To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) when shareholders are diversified, managers have incentives to cannibalize, and (2) option compensation reduces these cannibalization incentives.

(1) options are a better compensation tool than equity for firms that have diversified shareholders, and (2) options are more likely to be provided as compensation for managers of firms with lower insider and higher institutional ownership and lower leverage.

(1) when shareholders are diversified, options can reduce the agency costs that arise from the conflict between the goals of maximizing portfolio value and maximizing firm (equity value); (2) relative performance evaluation can destroy value when managers have an incentive to cannibalize; and (3) firms with lower insider and higher institutional ownership and lower leverage tend provide more options as compensation to their managers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of compensation contracts when shareholders are diversified.
the design of compensation contracts that reduce the incentive of managers to engage in cannabilistic activity.
the design of managerial compensation when shareholders are diversifying investors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of option compensation in firms is consistent with the predictions of a model that incorporates the conflict between shareholders and managers and the conflict between managers of diversified shareholders.

option grants are more effective in reducing cannibalization when the managers are more highly diversified, the firm has a lower level of insider ownership and higher level of institutional ownership, and the firm has less financial leverage.
options are a superior form of compensation when shareholders are more diversified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of stock option grants is more efficient when shareholders are diversified and when the firm has a higher level of institutional ownership.
option grants to managers are more effective than stock grants when shareholders are diversified and that option grants are less effective when the firm is more highly leveraged.

options are more valuable to shareholders when shareholders are diversified, when managers are less likely to be aligned with the interests of shareholders, and when firms are more likely to engage in cannabalization of their shareholders' wealth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the optimal mix of equity-based compensation and cash compensation is not the same across firms and that the relative importance of equity-based compensation increases when shareholders are less concentrated.
the design of executive compensation should be informed by an understanding of the incentives created by the compensation plan.
option grants may have an important role in corporate governance, particularly in large, publicly traded companies.
